name.en: Fake Inland Revenue message: “claim your tax refund”

how.en: Around the end of the tax year, emails, texts and fake social media accounts pretend to be Inland Revenue. They mention a refund amount or a tax bill and ask you to click a link to myIR, open an attachment or call a number. The goal is your myIR login, personal details or money. Inland Revenue never puts links to myIR or refund amounts in emails or texts.

text.en: A message or social post looks like it is from Inland Revenue.
It mentions a refund amount or a bill to pay.
It asks you to log in to myIR through a link.
The fake page takes your myIR login, details or card.
Inland Revenue: You are eligible for a tax refund of $512.80. Log in to myIR to confirm your bank account before 30 June: [link]

pt: recebi um sms falso da inland revenue
me mandaram um link estranho por e-mail
disseram que eu tinha dinheiro para receber
tentaram roubar minha senha do myir
perfil falso no facebook fingindo ser o fisco
pediram para ligar para um numero desconhecido
es: me llego un mensaje de inland revenue
me piden mis datos de miir
dice que tengo un saldo a favor
me llaman diciendo que debo dinero

en: A refund amount in an email or text.
A text from a normal mobile or overseas number.
An email that doesn’t end in ird.govt.nz.
Never use a link to log in to myIR: type ird.govt.nz yourself.
Refunds go straight to the bank account Inland Revenue already has.
If you shared details, contact Inland Revenue and your bank.

sources.title: Be alert to scammers this 2026 tax season
